title: Investigatio motuum, quibus laminae et virgae elasticae contremiscunt

deep.reconstruction:
Context. In Scholion §52 (begun on p.158) Euler claims that a naturally curved rod needs no new theory. Take the curve EXF itself as the axis, arc length s, and let y be the displacement normal to the curve. Then -y'' is the excess of curvature over the natural curvature, and the straight-beam equation (1/2g) y_tt = -b c^2 y_ssss still holds. So for a rod of length a with free, simply supported or clamped ends, all the tones found earlier for straight rods carry over unchanged.

This page. Euler finishes that claim ('nulla noua inuestigatione sit opus'). He then singles out the one case with no straight analogue: a rod whose natural shape closes on itself. This is the elastic ring, which he adds as a 'coronis' (crowning appendix).

§53 sets up the problem.
- Take a circle AXBC, or any closed curve, of total perimeter a, with the same thickness and elasticity as before.
- For a 'regular motion' (normal mode) let k be the length of the isochronous simple pendulum, and put f = (b c^2 k)^{1/4}.
- Let AX = s, and let X be displaced to Y at time t.
- The general modal solution is Y = C sin(ζ + t√(2g/k)) (α e^{s/f} + β e^{-s/f} + γ sin(s/f) + δ cos(s/f)).
- The whole task is now to fix α, β, γ, δ. The ring has no ends, so none of the earlier end conditions apply; closure must replace them.

The next page completes the argument. It requires y = 0 at s = 0, a, 2a, 3a, …, which forces α = β = δ = 0 and sin(iω) = 0, so ω = a/f = iπ. The tones are then i^2 π c √(2gb)/a^2, i.e. in the ratios 1 : 4 : 9 : 16 ….

In modern terms: Euler treats the ring as an Euler–Bernoulli beam of length a with periodic conditions, ignoring the coupling of curvature with tangential displacement and inextensibility.
errors: Physical error in §52, carried into §53. For a naturally curved rod the bending equation is not the straight-beam equation in arc-length coordinates. Curvature couples normal and tangential displacement (with inextensibility, w = -u'), and the change of curvature is not just -y''. For a ring of radius R the correct inextensional flexural frequencies are proportional to n(n^2-1)/√(n^2+1) (Hoppe 1871). Euler's model instead gives frequencies ∝ n^2. It also misses that n = 1 (rigid translation) has zero frequency.

Mathematical gap (completed on the next page). Requiring only y = 0 at s = 0, a, 2a, … does not impose periodicity. For a closed ring y and all its s-derivatives must be a-periodic, so a/f = 2πn, not nπ. With ω = iπ and i odd, sin(s/f) changes sign of slope at the junction s = a ≡ 0, which is inadmissible. The admissible tones are only the even-i members of Euler's list, i.e. ratios 4 : 16 : 36 …. Each also has a degenerate cos partner (choosing δ = 0 by placing A at a node is legitimate).
For a non-circular closed curve the claim that only the perimeter matters is likewise unjustified, since the local curvature enters the true equations.

ideas.what: Treating a naturally curved rod as a straight beam whose axis is the curve itself, with the same 4th-order equation in arc length.
ideas.modern_name: Naive (curvature-neglecting) curved-beam approximation; contrast with the Kirchhoff/Love curved-rod theory
ideas.usually_credited_to: Correct curved-rod and ring vibration theory: Hoppe (1871), Rayleigh, Love
ideas.where_published: E526 §52, Acta Acad. Sci. Petropol. 1779 (publ. 1782); O.O. II.11

ideas.what: Vibration of an elastic ring as a closed rod with no ends, replacing end conditions by closure conditions.
ideas.modern_name: Flexural vibrations of a ring; periodic boundary conditions for the Euler–Bernoulli beam
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (bell/ring model in 'Tentamen de sono campanarum', E303, 1766); correct theory Hoppe 1871

ideas.what: Normal-mode separation y = C sin(ζ + t√(2g/k)) X(s), with X a combination of e^{±s/f}, sin(s/f), cos(s/f), where f^4 = b c^2 k.
ideas.modern_name: Separation of variables for the beam equation; eigenfunctions of d^4/ds^4
ideas.where_published: E526 earlier sections; E65 (Methodus inveniendi, Additamentum I)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is the routine set-up of Euler's (physically flawed) ring-vibration problem. Euler's ring and bell work and its shortcomings are discussed in the standard histories, so nothing new is visible here. The periodicity slip (nπ instead of 2nπ) is a minor error that appears on the next page.
transcription_corrections: In the displayed equation the image has capital 'Y' on the left (Y = C sin. …), as in the transcription. Exponents read e^{s/f} and e^{-s/f}; 'sin. s/f + δ cos. s/f' is correct.
Margin note 'Tab. III. Fig. 10.' belongs beside the opening of §53.
'coronidis loco' is correctly read (the scan shows 'co-ronidis').
